name: The Outlaw Math
author: Transcribed from spoken performance by Cerise Vault, attributed; circulated via the Gray Zone print network, authorship disputed by at least one person who claims they wrote the ending
description: Transcription of a spoken piece delivered at The Drip Bar in Narrows Block 7 during an open-mic night sometime in the last eighteen months. The speaker, identified variously as 'Cerise Vault' and 'the woman with the jaw chrome and the green coat,' delivered an improvised-seeming but clearly rehearsed philosophical argument about freelancer moral reasoning. The piece was transcribed by at least three separate audience members; this version is a composite with interjections noted. Circulated in the Gray Zone print network, stapled into zine collections, left at several dead drops as what one broker described as 'a note with no job attached.' Some people leave it. Some people take it. Nobody knows what that means.
body:
I want to talk about the math.

Not economics. Not politics. Not the speech you've heard a hundred times about exploitation and the corps and why everything is the way it is. You know that speech. You've given that speech. I've given that speech. It doesn't get anyone fed.

I want to talk about the math you actually do. The math you do at three in the morning when a broker pings you and you're sitting in a the Gray Zone unit with forty-two square meters and two other people and the job is — whatever the job is. And you run the numbers. Not on a spreadsheet. In your chest. You run them in your chest and your hands and the particular quality of the silence in the room.

How much. Who gets hurt. How bad. Is it me or is it them. Can I live with it. Can I not live without it.

That's the math. That's what I want to talk about.

[Someone near the back said: that's just ethics. That's just regular ethics. The speaker said: hold on. Stay with me.]

Here's the lie I want to kill tonight. The lie is that freelancers are outlaws. That we're outside the system. That when you do the math — when you weigh the harm, when you decide what's acceptable and what isn't, when you sign on for something ugly because the alternative is uglier — that you're doing something different from what everyone else is doing. That you're morally alien. That the violence is yours specifically and the system is separate from it.

Areturus Civil Security has a harm-per-incident budget. I know this because someone I trust has seen it. It's a spreadsheet. Actual spreadsheet. How much property crime is acceptable before deployment costs exceed losses. How many assaults in the Gray Zone Block 14 before it's cheaper to respond than to absorb. They run the math. They run it constantly. The difference between their math and yours is that theirs has a compliance department and a legal team and nobody calls it morality because they don't have to.

The executives who own the Canopy towers that suck heat from the lower stacks — they have committees. Return on investment versus community stability risk. Long-term infrastructure depreciation versus quarterly targets. Harm on one side of the ledger. Profit on the other. Acceptable loss. They run it every Tuesday. There's probably a standing agenda item.

You run it at three in the morning in forty-two square meters with your hands shaking and you think you're doing something different from them.

You're not outside the system. You are a mechanism of the system. A small one. An informal one. A deniable one. But the math you're doing is the same math that runs the entire city. The only difference — the only difference — is that you're doing it explicitly. You're doing it without a committee. Without the legal language that turns 'acceptable loss' into 'resource allocation.' Without the institutional frame that makes the numbers disappear into a document nobody reads.

[A man near the front — I think his name is Garrow, someone said Garrow — said: so what? If it's all the same math, what does it matter how you run it? The speaker paused. This is where she slowed down.]

It matters because you can see it.

That's the whole thing. That's the entire argument. When you're sitting with the job in your chest at three in the morning, you cannot make it invisible. You cannot outsource the weight of it to a committee. You cannot file it. You cannot put it in a quarterly report and walk away. You have to hold it. You are the committee. You are the compliance department. You are the legal team. And you are also the person who has to sleep afterward.

This is not a gift. I'm not romanticizing it. This is a brutal tax on people who were already overtaxed. The corporations outsourced their guilt along with everything else and the cost landed on us. I'm not grateful for the clarity. I'd trade it for a standing agenda item and a salary, same as anyone.

But since we can't — since the math is ours to carry — I'm saying it can be done better and it can be done worse.

Better doesn't mean clean. Better doesn't mean you find the job that harms no one, because that job doesn't exist, and anyone who's been working more than six months knows that. Better means you see the numbers clearly. Better means you don't average away the person on the other side of the harm into a category. Better means you ask the question — actually ask it, not as ritual — whether there's a version of this that costs less in the places that matter.

Some people run the math and they're honest about it. I've worked with people who will tell you exactly what they'll do and exactly what they won't and the line is real and they hold it. I've worked with people who don't run it at all, who've decided the question is too expensive, who've replaced the math with a story — the story where they're the outlaw, the story where the corps are so evil that whatever they do in response is justified, the story where survival erases the ledger. Those people are dangerous. Not because they're bad. Because they stopped looking at the numbers.

[Someone, I didn't catch who, said: you're asking people to feel guilty for surviving. The speaker said: No. I'm asking people to know what they're doing.]

Guilt is not the point. Guilt is what you feel when you've absorbed the system's framing and it tells you that your pain is your fault. The math is not guilt. The math is information. The math is: this job, this cost, this necessity, this specific person who gets hurt, this specific reason. Holding that information doesn't mean you don't take the job. It means you took the job and you knew what you were taking.

I believe that matters. I believe it matters not because the universe rewards it, not because the Signal Network cares, not because it makes you safer or better paid or longer-lived. I believe it matters because it is the only form of honesty available to us. Because we are doing the same work the city does and we are doing it without the machinery of invisibility and we can at least refuse to pretend otherwise.

The outlaw frame is a comfort. It says: I am outside this. It says: the violence I do is rebellion and the violence done to me is oppression and there's a clean story here with me on the right side of it. I understand why people reach for it. I have reached for it. It is warm and it is a lie.

You're not an outlaw. You're a laborer in an informal economy doing harm-benefit calculus without institutional support, without legal protection, without a pension, in a world that will kill you and feel nothing about it.

The math is yours.

Do it honestly.

Do it like it counts.

[End of transcription. Note from one of the transcribers: she left before anyone could talk to her. Someone said she walked to the Gray Zone line. Someone else said she didn't. Nobody agrees on the jaw chrome.]
